subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
The Thursday review room was quiet. Elizabeth sat at the far end with her laptop closed, shoulders hunched. She had been the one who ran the command that wiped the live data.
Ayesha, leading the meeting, wrote a question on the whiteboard: "Why did one command wipe the live data?" Then she turned to face the room. "Not who. Why does our set-up let a single person do this in one step?"
The list grew line by line. Everyone on the team had full delete rights. The test and live screens looked almost the same. Nothing asked, "Are you sure?" before the command ran.
Elizabeth looked up for the first time. "So it could have been anyone."
"Yes," Ayesha said. "Let's fix that."

qa.q: What did Ayesha write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Ayesha wrote a question asking why one command wiped the live data.

qa.q: What was Ayesha likely feeling as she turned from the whiteboard to the room?
qa.a: Ayesha was calm and purposeful, wanting the team to look at the set-up instead of blaming a person.

qa.q: What could the team do next about the three gaps on the list?
qa.a: They could assign an owner and a date to each gap: limit delete rights, make test and live look different, and add a confirmation step.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt when the list showed it could have been anyone?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt relief and less alone, shown by looking up for the first time after sitting hunched.

grounding: The passage shows a team asking why the set-up allowed one command to remove live data and finding weak permissions, similar-looking screens and no confirmation step.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage:
Hi Jasleen,
I wanted to write after yesterday's review, because you looked like you hadn't slept.
Here's what we found, and I want you to read it slowly. We didn't ask 'who ran the command?' We asked 'why could one command delete production data at all?' The answers were about the system, not you:
1. Your account had full delete rights on production, which a new engineer should never have been given.
2. The tool didn't ask for confirmation before dropping a table.
3. Test and production looked identical in the terminal.
Any of us could have made that slip on that setup. You just happened to be the one at the keyboard.
We've assigned fixes for all three. I'd like you to own the confirmation step, if you're up for it.
Hansa

qa.q: What was the second finding of the review?
qa.a: The tool didn't ask for confirmation before dropping a table.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling at the review?
qa.a: Jasleen was likely ashamed and exhausted, looking like someone who hadn't slept after the deletion.

qa.q: Why is it wise for Hansa to offer Jasleen the confirmation step?
qa.a: It turns the mistake into a chance to fix the system, helping Jasleen rebuild confidence instead of carrying blame.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see a review that asks 'why' instead of 'who'?
qa.a: They are more likely to feel safe reporting their own slips, knowing the focus will be on fixing the system.

grounding: It shows a review asking why the system let one command delete production data and finding missing safeguards, weak permissions and no confirmation step.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
passage: Lavanya, you asked what our worst outage taught me. Okay. Last April a junior on my team ran a script that wiped the orders table in production. The next day, in the review, I could see everyone waiting for me to name him. I didn't. I'm Sonali, and I'd been that junior once. So I wrote on the whiteboard: 'Why was this possible?' And we just kept asking why. Why did his account have delete rights on production? Because permissions were copied from a senior's profile. Why didn't the script stop? Because there was no confirmation step. Why couldn't he tell test from production? Because the prompts looked the same. By the end, the whiteboard had three fixes and no names. And the next month, the junior was the first to report a near miss.

qa.q: What did Sonali write on the whiteboard?
Why didn't Sonali name the junior, and how does Sonali seem to feel about that choice?
qa.a: Remembering being that junior once, Sonali felt empathy, and seems proud that the review ended with fixes and no names.

qa.q: What else could the team do with the three fixes?
qa.a: They could give each fix an owner and a date, and check a month later that the confirmation step and permissions actually changed.

qa.q: How did the review affect the junior?
qa.a: The junior was spared public blame and, a month later, felt safe enough to be the first to report a near miss.

grounding: It shows a blameless review asking why one command could remove production data and finding weak permissions, no confirmation step and look-alike environments.
